task_title: Regulations and Publications Related to IFR Operations
objective: By the end of this lesson you can describe, for 14 CFR parts 61, 71, 91, 95 and 97, the Instrument Flying Handbook, the AIM, the PTS and ACS, the Chart Supplement, SIDs and STARs, en route charts and approach charts, what each is for, what it holds, where to get it and how it is revised. You can tell a learner which ones are binding, prove that every document in the flight bag is current, and teach a learner to find an IFR answer in the right document.
why: An instrument rating applicant must receive and log ground training from an authorized instructor, or complete a home-study course, on the IFR regulations, the IFR information in the AIM, and the use of IFR en route and approach charts [[60:250|14 CFR 61.65(b)]]. When you give an IPC, you check the same things: part 91 and the reading of SID, ODP, STAR and approach charts [[15:31|AC 61-98E 5.2.1]]. If you already hold a flight instructor certificate with an airplane rating, the FAA-S-8081-9E table for adding an instrument rating lists this Task as required in Area II [[FAA-S-8081-9E:18|PTS Additional Rating Table]]. And because aeronautical information changes fast, using current editions is a safety issue, not paperwork [[2:6|Chart Users' Guide p 6]].

warmup: Think first: your instrument learner arrives with a printed 2012 Instrument Flying Handbook, an AIM marked Change 2, and a tablet whose chart subscription lapsed three weeks ago. He says, "The AIM tells me to fly the obstacle departure, so that's the law, right?" Which of his documents are still good, which ones bind him, and how would you prove each one is current?

key_terms.def: Outside material made part of 14 CFR without printing it there, approved by the Director of the Federal Register; FAA Order JO 7400.11M and the ACS/PTS are examples [[60:411|14 CFR 71.1]] [[60:199|14 CFR 61.14]].
Standard instrument approach procedure. Part 97 prescribes SIAPs to civil airports and the weather minimums for landing under IFR there [[60:723|14 CFR 97.1]] [[60:725|14 CFR 97.3]].

Minimum en route IFR altitude on an ATS route or segment; it applies to the entire width of the route [[60:712|14 CFR 95.1(d)]] and gives adequate navigation signal reception and obstacle clearance [[23:25|IFH 1-6]].
Minimum obstruction clearance altitude: obstruction clearance, with VOR reception assured only within 22 NM of the VOR [[60:712|14 CFR 95.1(e)]].
Where to switch from the navaid behind to the next one [[60:712|14 CFR 95.1(g)]]; unless otherwise specified, midway on a straight segment [[60:722|14 CFR 95.8001]].
Obstacle departure procedure, textual or graphic; it may be flown without an ATC clearance unless ATC assigns a SID or radar vectors [[33:349|AIM 5-2-9]].
Standard instrument departure: an ATC procedure, always graphic; an ATC clearance must be received before flying it [[33:349|AIM 5-2-9]].
An ATC coded IFR arrival route that simplifies clearance delivery and links the en route structure to the approach [[33:393|AIM 5-4-1]].
Civil/military flight information publication issued every 56 days, with airport, NAVAID and communications data and what cannot be readily charted [[34:199|AIM 9-1-5]].
U.S. Terminal Procedures Publication: approach charts, DPs, STARs, charted visual procedures and airport diagrams, plus takeoff, radar and alternate minimums [[2:97|Chart Users' Guide p 97]].
Julian date in an approach chart's top margin: first two digits the year, last three the day of the year [[2:100|Chart Users' Guide p 100]].
The table in each AIM change listing the pages to remove and the dated pages to insert [[33:39|AIM Table: Change 3 Page Control Chart]].

chunks.title: The map: what each document is for, and which ones bind

body.p: FAA-S-8081-9E asks you to describe each of these documents by its purpose, general content, availability and method of revision, related to instrument flight and instrument instruction [[FAA-S-8081-9E:27|PTS II.C]]. Give a learner the whole map first, then open one document at a time. The CFI lesson AI.II.J shows how 14 CFR is built and how ACs and the POH fit in, and the Instrument lesson IR.I.A covers pilot qualifications. This lesson adds the IFR documents and how to prove each one is current.

callout.text: Four questions for every document, in the PTS order: what is it for, what is in it, where do I get it, and how do I know mine is current?

check.q: A learner says, "If it's in the AIM, it's a regulation." What do you answer?
check.a: The AIM says it is not regulatory; it shows techniques and procedures that other regulations may require [[33:53|AIM Flight Information Publication Policy]]. Find the rule in 14 CFR first, then use the AIM for how to comply.

chunks.title: K1: Part 61, the IFR pilot and the instrument instructor

body.p: Part 61 says who may act as pilot in command under IFR and who may teach it. To act as PIC under IFR, or in weather below VFR minimums, a pilot needs the category, class and instrument rating on the pilot certificate, or an ATP certificate [[60:191|14 CFR 61.3(e)]]. He also needs recent experience: six approaches, holding, and intercepting and tracking courses within the 6 calendar months before the month of the flight [[60:239|14 CFR 61.57(c)(1)]]. Once more than six calendar months behind, only an IPC restores it, covering the areas of operation of the applicable ACS [[60:240|14 CFR 61.57(d)(1)]].

head: Section
Why it matters to a CFII
rows: The learner must receive and log ground training from an authorized instructor, or complete a home-study course, on the IFR regulations, the IFR information in the AIM, and IFR en route and approach charts, among other areas. This Task is that ground school [[60:250|14 CFR 61.65(b)]].

An instrument rating on a flight instructor certificate requires a commercial or ATP certificate with an instrument rating, or instrument privileges, appropriate to the rating sought [[60:339|14 CFR 61.183(c)]].
You must receive and log ground training on the instrument rating knowledge areas for the category [[60:340|14 CFR 61.185(a)(3)]].
The flight proficiency areas for the instructor instrument rating begin with fundamentals of instructing and technical subject areas [[60:344|14 CFR 61.187(b)(7)]].

Instrument training for an instrument rating, and the instrument training required for commercial and ATP certificates, needs an instrument rating on your flight instructor certificate [[60:346|14 CFR 61.195(c)]].
You may not endorse an IPC unless you tested the pilot under 61.57(d) [[60:347|14 CFR 61.195(d)(6)]].
The CFII PTS and the instrument ACS are incorporated by reference, and the practical test is their tasks [[60:200|14 CFR 61.14(a)(4)]] [[60:222|14 CFR 61.43(a)(1)]].

body.p: Teach the learner where these live. 61.57 is in Subpart A, General [[60:183|14 CFR 61.1]]; 61.65 is in Subpart B, Aircraft Ratings and Pilot Authorizations [[60:245|14 CFR 61.61]]; your own instructor rules start Subpart H at 61.181 [[60:338|14 CFR 61.181]]. The Logbook Task, FII.II.D, covers the endorsements and records.

callout.text: Application: open with the learner's own question, "Can I go IFR next month?", and answer it from 61.3(e) and 61.57(c) together. Then show the 61.65(b) list so the learner sees why today's lesson is on the syllabus.

check.q: A commercial pilot with an instrument rating but a CFI certificate without one asks if he can give the instrument training a commercial applicant needs. What do you show him?
check.a: No. 61.195(c) requires an instrument rating on the flight instructor certificate for that training [[60:346|14 CFR 61.195(c)]].

chunks.title: K1: Part 91 before the flight: the IFR planning rules

body.p: Part 91 Subpart B holds the flight rules [[60:440|14 CFR 91.101]], and its Instrument Flight Rules group starts at 91.167 [[60:468|14 CFR 91.167]]. With the preflight rule, the safety pilot rule, the IFR equipment list and two inspection rules, these are the sections a learner plans with. For the same reason, the instructor giving an IPC checks knowledge of part 91 Subparts B, C and E [[15:31|AC 61-98E 5.2.1]].

head: Rule
What it requires
rows: 91.103(a) Preflight action
For an IFR flight: weather reports and forecasts, fuel requirements, alternatives if the flight cannot be completed, and known ATC traffic delays [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103(a)]]
91.109(c) Safety pilot

A safety pilot with at least a private certificate with category and class ratings, adequate vision forward and to each side or a competent observer, and fully functioning dual controls [[60:446|14 CFR 91.109(c)(1)]] [[60:447|14 CFR 91.109(c)(2)]] [[60:447|14 CFR 91.109(c)(3)]]
91.167 Fuel
Fuel to the first airport of intended landing, then to the alternate if one is required, then 45 minutes at normal cruising speed [[60:468|14 CFR 91.167(a)(1)]] [[60:469|14 CFR 91.167(a)(2)]]
91.169(b) Alternate required?

No alternate if part 97 prescribes an approach at the first airport of intended landing and, from 1 hour before to 1 hour after ETA, the ceiling will be at least 2,000 feet and visibility at least 3 statute miles [[60:469|14 CFR 91.169(b)]]
91.169(c) Alternate minimums

The alternate minimums on the procedure, or 600 and 2 (precision) or 800 and 2 (nonprecision); with no approach, descent from the MEA, approach and landing under basic VFR [[60:470|14 CFR 91.169(c)(1)]] [[60:470|14 CFR 91.169(c)(2)]]
91.171 VOR check

Within the preceding 30 days: plus or minus 4 degrees with a test signal or ground checkpoint, 6 degrees airborne, 4 degrees between dual VORs; log date, place and bearing error, and sign [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(a)]] [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(b)]] [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(c)]] [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(d)]]
91.173 Clearance
IFR in controlled airspace needs a filed IFR flight plan and an appropriate ATC clearance [[60:471|14 CFR 91.173]]
91.205(d) IFR equipment

VFR (and night) items plus two-way radio and navigation equipment suitable for the route, rate-of-turn and slip-skid indicators, a sensitive altimeter, a clock with seconds, an adequate generator or alternator, an attitude indicator and a directional gyro [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)]]

Static system, altimeter and altitude reporting tested within 24 calendar months for IFR in controlled airspace; transponder within 24 calendar months [[60:524|14 CFR 91.411(a)(1)]] [[60:525|14 CFR 91.413(a)]]

callout.text: Alternate check: an approach at the destination, then 1 hour either side of ETA, a 2,000-foot ceiling and 3 miles. All true: no alternate required [[60:469|14 CFR 91.169(b)]].

body.p: The Instrument lesson IR.I.C puts these rules into a real flight plan. Here the goal is speed: the learner should open part 91 and land on the right section in seconds.

check.q: A learner asks whether a VOR check made 35 days ago is good for tomorrow's IFR flight. What do you say and show?
check.a: Not unless the VOR is maintained under an approved procedure. 91.171(a) requires an operational check within the preceding 30 days; show him the tolerances and how to log a new one [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(a)]] [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(d)]].

chunks.title: K1: Part 91 in the air: clearances, altitudes, approaches and failures

body.p: Once the airplane is in the system, these sections govern the flight. In an IPC you also check the pilot's grasp of ATC procedures under IFR, with emphasis on clearances and pilot and controller responsibilities [[15:32|AC 61-98E 5.2.1]].

head: Rule
What it requires
rows: 91.123 Clearances
No deviation without an amended clearance, an emergency or a TCAS resolution advisory; if uncertain, ask ATC at once [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(a)]]
91.135 Class A
IFR only, under a clearance received before entering [[60:456|14 CFR 91.135(a)]]
91.175(a) to (c) Approaches

Use the part 97 SIAP; the authorized DA/DH or MDA is the highest of the procedure's, the PIC's and the equipment's; go below it only when continuously in position for a normal descent, with the required flight visibility and a listed visual reference [[60:471|14 CFR 91.175(a)]] [[60:471|14 CFR 91.175(b)]] [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(1)]]
91.175(e) Missed approach

Miss immediately when those conditions are not met below the MDA or at the missed approach point or DA/DH, or when an identifiable part of the airport is lost while circling [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(e)]] [[60:473|14 CFR 91.175(e)(2)]]
91.177 Minimum altitudes

Not below the part 95 and 97 altitudes; below the MEA down to the MOCA only with signals, and on VOR only within 22 NM; with no published altitude, 2,000 feet above the highest obstacle within 4 NM in a mountainous area, 1,000 feet elsewhere [[60:480|14 CFR 91.177(a)]]
91.179 Cruising altitude

In controlled airspace, the altitude ATC assigns; in uncontrolled airspace below 18,000 MSL, odd thousands for 0 to 179 degrees magnetic and even thousands for 180 to 359 [[60:480|14 CFR 91.179(a)]] [[60:481|14 CFR 91.179(b)]]
91.181 Course
On an ATS route, the centerline; otherwise the direct course between the fixes [[60:482|14 CFR 91.181]]
91.183 Reports
Continuous listening watch; report reporting points (under radar control only those requested), unforecast weather, and other safety information [[60:482|14 CFR 91.183]]
91.185 Lost communications

In VFR conditions, continue VFR and land as soon as practicable; in IFR, the route and altitude priorities and the clearance limit rules [[60:482|14 CFR 91.185(b)]] [[60:482|14 CFR 91.185(c)(1)]] [[60:483|14 CFR 91.185(c)(2)]] [[60:483|14 CFR 91.185(c)(3)]]
91.187 Malfunctions

In controlled airspace, report in-flight malfunctions of navigation, approach or communication equipment: aircraft ID, equipment affected, degree of impairment and assistance desired [[60:483|14 CFR 91.187]]

callout.text: Read the first sentence of 91.175(f). Its takeoff minimums and ODP rule apply to persons operating under parts 121, 125, 129 or 135 [[60:473|14 CFR 91.175(f)]]. A part 91 pilot who departs IFR without an ODP, SID or DVA is responsible for obstacle clearance [[33:354|AIM 5-2-9]], and the AIM strongly encourages filing and flying a DP at night, in marginal VMC and in IMC [[33:349|AIM 5-2-9]].

body.p: Deeper lessons: FII.IX.A teaches the 91.185 lost-communication rule, and IR.VI.A and IR.VI.C apply 91.175 to approaches and missed approaches.

check.q: Your learner, navigating by VOR only, wants to descend to the MOCA 30 NM from the VOR that defines the airway. Legal?
check.a: No. Below the MEA down to the MOCA is allowed only with the navigation signals available, and with VOR only within 22 NM of the VOR [[60:480|14 CFR 91.177(a)]] [[60:712|14 CFR 95.1(e)]].

chunks.title: K1: Part 71, and how 14 CFR is revised

body.p: Part 71 designates Class A, B, C, D and E airspace, air traffic service routes and reporting points. It is short because the listings themselves are in FAA Order JO 7400.11M, Airspace Designations and Reporting Points, incorporated by reference [[60:411|14 CFR 71.1]].

bullets: Class A: from 18,000 feet MSL to and including FL600 over the 48 states and within 12 NM of their coast [[60:414|14 CFR 71.33(a)]]; part 91 sets its rating, operating and equipment rules [[60:413|14 CFR 71.31]], starting with IFR under a clearance [[60:456|14 CFR 91.135(a)]].

Class E includes 14,500 feet MSL up to but not including 18,000 feet, and the airspace above FL600 [[60:416|14 CFR 71.71(a)]]; areas from 700 feet AGL or more around an airport with an approved instrument approach, or from 1,200 feet or more for transitions [[60:416|14 CFR 71.71(c)]]; and the Federal airways [[60:416|14 CFR 71.71(d)]].
ATS routes: jet routes and RNAV routes in subpart A; VOR Federal airways, colored Federal airways and RNAV routes in subpart E [[60:412|14 CFR 71.13]].
Bearings and radials in part 71 are true, and mileages are nautical miles [[60:412|14 CFR 71.7]].
Where designations overlap, the rules of the more restrictive airspace apply [[60:412|14 CFR 71.9(a)]].

body.p: **How the listings change.** Proposed changes are published as proposed rules, and amendments as final rules, in the Federal Register; periodically they are folded into a new edition of the Order. JO 7400.11M, dated July 30, 2026, is incorporated from September 15, 2026, through September 15, 2027, and is on the FAA website [[60:411|14 CFR 71.1]].

**How to read the version of 14 CFR you have.** The CFR in this library is the eCFR, which calls itself authoritative but unofficial, and every page shows its "up to date as of" date, here 10/08/2026 [[60:711|14 CFR 95.1]]. The CFR, like the AIM and the FAA handbooks, is available on the FAA website [[29:5|IPH iii]].

bullets: Each section ends with its amendment history in brackets, with the Federal Register volume, page and date, for example Amdt. 71-58, 91 FR 55739, Aug. 31, 2026 [[60:411|14 CFR 71.1]].
An Effective Date Note flags a change and when it takes effect [[60:411|14 CFR 71.1]].

An Editorial Note sends you to the List of CFR Sections Affected for material not carried in the CFR, such as part 95 route altitudes and part 97 procedures [[60:722|14 CFR 95.31]] [[60:726|14 CFR 97.20]].
Incorporated documents carry their own edition and date: FAA-S-8081-9E and FAA-S-ACS-8C, both November 2023 [[60:200|14 CFR 61.14(a)(4)]] [[60:200|14 CFR 61.14(b)(5)]].

callout.text: Application: before a ground lesson, check the "up to date as of" date on every page of regulation you hand out, and teach the learner to do the same. An old printout of 61.57 or 91.175 teaches an old rule.

check.q: A learner compares the bearings in a part 71 airway description with the courses in part 97 and asks why they seem to use different references. What do you say?
check.a: Part 71 bearings and radials are true [[60:412|14 CFR 71.7]], while part 97 courses are magnetic unless otherwise designated [[60:725|14 CFR 97.5(a)]]. Teach her which part she is reading before she compares numbers.

chunks.title: K1: Parts 95 and 97, the IFR altitudes and the procedures

body.p: Part 95 prescribes the altitudes for IFR on ATS routes and other direct routes with an MEA, and designates mountainous areas and changeover points [[60:711|14 CFR 95.1(a)]]. Teach each altitude by its definition, then by its chart symbol.

head: Altitude
What 95.1 says
On the en route chart
rows: MEA
Minimum en route IFR altitude; covers the entire width of the route; off-airway, 4 NM each side unless otherwise specified [[60:712|14 CFR 95.1(d)]]
Signal reception and obstacle clearance, typically 1,000 feet, 2,000 feet in designated mountainous areas; "MEA GAP" where coverage breaks [[23:25|IFH 1-6]]
MOCA
Obstruction clearance, with VOR reception assured only within 22 NM of the VOR [[60:712|14 CFR 95.1(e)]]
Below the MEA with a leading asterisk, such as *3400 [[23:25|IFH 1-6]]
MRA
Lowest altitude at which an intersection can be determined with ground-based navaids [[60:712|14 CFR 95.1(f)]]
"MRA" and the altitude; with DME, the fix may be identified below it if the chart shows DME is authorized [[23:25|IFH 1-6]] [[23:26|IFH 1-7]]
MCA
For proceeding to a higher MEA when crossing specified fixes [[60:712|14 CFR 95.1(c)]]
Airway, altitude and direction, such as "V24 8000 SE"; reach it by the fix [[23:26|IFH 1-7]]
MAA
Highest altitude at which adequate VOR reception is assured [[60:712|14 CFR 95.1(b)]]
COP
Where to change from the navaid behind to the next one [[60:712|14 CFR 95.1(g)]]; midway on straight segments unless otherwise specified [[60:722|14 CFR 95.8001]]
COP symbol with distances; no symbol means change midway [[23:29|IFH 1-10]]

body.p: The altitude for each route and the changeover points are not printed in the CFR; editorial notes in part 95 say so and point to the Federal Register [[60:722|14 CFR 95.31]] [[60:722|14 CFR 95.8001]]. Pilots read them on the en route charts, which show MEAs, MOCAs and reporting points [[34:194|AIM 9-1-5]].

Part 97 prescribes standard instrument approach procedures to civil airports with their landing minimums, and obstacle departure procedures with IFR takeoff minimums [[60:723|14 CFR 97.1]]. 97.3 defines the symbols and terms the procedures use: approach categories by VREF, or 1.3 VSO if no VREF is set (A under 91 knots; B 91 to less than 121; C 121 to less than 141; D 141 to less than 166; E 166 or more), the approach segments, the MSA with at least 1,000 feet of obstacle clearance for emergency use, NoPT and the procedure turn [[60:724|14 CFR 97.3]] [[60:725|14 CFR 97.3]].

Part 97 does not print the procedures either. They are documented on FAA Forms 8260-3, 8260-4 and 8260-5 (ODPs and takeoff minimums on 8260-15A), incorporated by reference, built to the TERPS criteria of FAA Order 8260.3, and depicted on FAA charts available on the FAA website [[60:726|14 CFR 97.20]]. When an instrument approach to a civil airport is needed, 91.175(a) requires the part 97 procedure [[60:471|14 CFR 91.175(a)]].

callout.text: Application: three layers in one minute. Find an MEA on the chart, read 95.1(d) for what it means, then 91.177 for why it binds the pilot. Do the same with a DA on an approach chart, 97.3 and 91.175.

check.q: What does an MSA promise the pilot?
check.a: At least 1,000 feet of obstacle clearance within the stated distance of the facility or fix, for emergency use [[60:725|14 CFR 97.3]].

chunks.title: K2: The Instrument Flying Handbook and its companion, the IPH

body.p: The Instrument Flying Handbook, FAA-H-8083-15B, is designed for instrument flight instructors and for pilots preparing for instrument rating tests, as basic reference material for knowledge testing and instrument flight training [[23:6|IFH iii]]. It covers human and aerodynamic factors, the flight instruments, attitude instrument flying, basic maneuvers in IMC, navigation systems, the NAS, the ATC system, IFR flight procedures and IFR emergencies, plus clearance shorthand and an integrated instrument lesson guide [[23:6|IFH iii]]. That guide, Appendix B, gives the minimum training for adding an instrument rating to a private or commercial certificate [[23:11|IFH viii]].

bullets: **Binding?** No. Where it says "must", that wording is not meant to add to, interpret or relieve a duty imposed by 14 CFR [[23:6|IFH iii]].
**Availability:** sold by the Government Printing Office and available to download as a PDF from the FAA [[23:6|IFH iii]].

**Revision:** a new edition supersedes the old one; the 15B replaced the 2007 edition [[23:6|IFH iii]]. Between editions, an errata sheet on the FAA handbooks page lists content and grammar errors, to be corrected in the next version [[23:1|IFH errata note]].

body.p: The Instrument Procedures Handbook, FAA-H-8083-16B, expands and updates IFH information and adds advanced IFR material, with detailed coverage of charts and procedures from takeoff to landing. Instrument instructors and students use it, it is a reference for the instrument knowledge test and the practical test standards, and it superseded the 2015 edition [[29:5|IPH iii]].

callout.text: Application: assign the IFH for attitude flying, instruments and systems, and the IPH for procedures and charts. Teach the learner to check any rule, name or chart detail in a handbook against 14 CFR, the AIM and the Chart Users' Guide before trusting it.

check.q: Your learner quotes the IFH: currency is "within the preceding 6 months." How do you correct him?
check.a: Show 61.57(c)(1): the window is the 6 calendar months before the month of the flight [[60:239|14 CFR 61.57(c)(1)]]. The IFH introduction simplifies it [[23:11|IFH viii]], and the regulation controls.

chunks.title: K3: The Aeronautical Information Manual: what it is, what it holds, how it changes

body.p: The AIM is the official guide to basic flight information and ATC procedures for the U.S. NAS [[1:24|PHAK 1-9]]. Its policy statement says it is not regulatory: it shows examples of techniques and procedures that may be requirements in other federal publications or regulations, to help pilots carry out those responsibilities. The same statement reminds pilots that the FAA does not promise to publish every hazard; being alert is the pilot's inherent responsibility [[33:53|AIM Flight Information Publication Policy]].

head: Paragraph
Use it to teach
rows: 1-1-4 VOR receiver check
VOTs, checkpoints and dual-VOR checks behind 91.171; their locations are in the Chart Supplement [[33:70|AIM 1-1-4]] [[33:71|AIM 1-1-4]]
Databases must be updated for IFR operations [[33:90|AIM 1-1-17]]
5-2-9 Departure procedures
ODPs, SIDs, diverse vector areas and the pilot's responsibilities [[33:349|AIM 5-2-9]] [[33:355|AIM 5-2-9]]
5-4-1 STARs
"Descend via", "expect" altitudes, chart possession and "NO STAR" [[33:393|AIM 5-4-1]] [[33:395|AIM 5-4-1]]
5-4-5 Approach charts
Part 97 SIAPs, civil versus military procedures, PPR [[33:397|AIM 5-4-5]]
9-1-5 Chart series
What each chart shows and how often it is revised [[34:190|AIM 9-1-5]]

body.p: **How it changes.** The AIM is a Basic manual plus three Changes. This cycle: Basic 2/20/25, Change 1 8/7/25, Change 2 1/22/26 and Change 3 7/9/26; the next Basic is effective 12/24/26 [[33:52|AIM Table: Publication Schedule]].

bullets: **Explanation of Changes:** the front of each change lists the changed paragraphs and why. Change 3 updated 5-1-2 (preload GPS waypoints on the ground), 5-4-5 (PPR can apply at civil airports) and 5-5-5 (missed approach wording), among others [[33:37|AIM Explanation of Changes]].
**Page Control Chart:** the pages to remove and the dated pages to insert [[33:39|AIM Table: Change 3 Page Control Chart]].
**Checklist of Pages:** the current date of every page [[33:42|AIM Table: Checklist of Pages]].
**Revision bars:** the Explanation of Changes even notes when they were left off because a change was insignificant [[33:37|AIM Explanation of Changes]].

**Availability:** posted on the FAA Air Traffic Plans and Publications website by its effective date and sent electronically to email subscribers; all organizations are responsible for subscribing to change notices [[33:50|AIM Subscription Information]].

callout.text: Today the current AIM is Change 3; a new Basic takes over on 12/24/26 [[33:52|AIM Table: Publication Schedule]]. Application: put that date in your calendar and recheck every paragraph you quote in your lesson plans.

check.q: How can a learner prove the AIM he studies is current?
check.a: Match its Basic or Change and date to the Publication Schedule [[33:52|AIM Table: Publication Schedule]], read the Explanation of Changes [[33:37|AIM Explanation of Changes]], and subscribe to change notices [[33:50|AIM Subscription Information]].

chunks.title: K4: The Practical Test Standards, the ACS and how this Task is tested

body.p: Your test uses FAA-S-8081-9E, Flight Instructor Instrument Practical Test Standards for Airplane Rating and Helicopter Rating, November 2023, incorporated by reference in part 61 [[60:200|14 CFR 61.14(a)(4)]]. A practical test consists of performing the tasks in the applicable ACS or PTS [[60:222|14 CFR 61.43(a)(1)]]. Your learners' instrument rating test and IPCs use FAA-S-ACS-8C, Instrument Rating Airplane ACS, November 2023 [[60:200|14 CFR 61.14(b)(5)]] [[60:240|14 CFR 61.57(d)(1)]]; for the IPC flight, AC 61-98E points to the ACS rating task table [[15:32|AC 61-98E 5.3]] [[FAA-S-ACS-8C:35|IR ACS Appendix 1]].

bullets: **Purpose:** written for FAA inspectors and evaluators; instructors use it to prepare applicants, and applicants refer to it in training [[FAA-S-8081-9E:7|PTS General Information]].
**Availability:** a PDF download from www.faa.gov; comments go to acsptsinquiries@faa.gov [[FAA-S-8081-9E:7|PTS General Information]].

**Revision:** the FAA revises it whenever changes are needed in the interest of safety; 9E superseded 9D with Changes 1 and 2 of July 2010 [[FAA-S-8081-9E:2|PTS Foreword]] [[FAA-S-8081-9E:7|PTS Concept]].
**Words:** "shall" and "must" are mandatory; "should" and "may" are guidance [[FAA-S-8081-9E:7|PTS General Information]].
**References:** maneuver descriptions come from the current issue of the listed references, as amended [[FAA-S-8081-9E:8|PTS Description]].

body.p: The ACS and PTS are testing documents, not a training syllabus, and the latest version with all changes should be used for training [[24:30|AFH 1-9]]. They are limited to the most critical job tasks, so a test does not represent an entire syllabus [[25:108|AIH 5-5]]. They are criterion-referenced, and their standards reflect 14 CFR and other FAA publications such as the AIM [[25:140|AIH 6-9]].

head: On your checkride
What FAA-S-8081-9E says
rows: Area II selection
The evaluator selects Tasks A and D and at least one other Task [[FAA-S-8081-9E:26|PTS Area II NOTE]].
Adding CFII to a CFI with an airplane rating
The addition table lists Area II Tasks A and C, and a listed Task is mandatory [[FAA-S-8081-9E:18|PTS Additional Rating Table]].
Question style
Oral questions at any time, scenario-based where possible, testing application and correlation [[FAA-S-8081-9E:13|PTS Evaluator Responsibility]] [[FAA-S-8081-9E:14|PTS Evaluator Responsibility]].
Instructional knowledge
Explanations should follow the teaching methods of the Aviation Instructor's Handbook [[FAA-S-8081-9E:10|PTS Use of the PTS]].

callout.text: FAA-S-8081-9E still says all instrument rating PTS procedures are included in it [[FAA-S-8081-9E:9|PTS Use of the PTS]], but the instrument rating now uses an ACS, FAA-S-ACS-8C [[60:200|14 CFR 61.14(b)(5)]]. Train your learners to the ACS.

check.q: Your instrument learner wants to use the ACS as his syllabus. What do you tell him?
check.a: Use it to set lesson standards, but it is a testing document, not a syllabus [[24:30|AFH 1-9]], and it covers only the most critical tasks [[25:108|AIH 5-5]].

body.p: The Chart Supplement is a series of civil/military flight information publications issued by the FAA every 56 days: Chart Supplement U.S., Alaska and Pacific. The U.S. edition is 7 volumes covering the conterminous U.S., Puerto Rico and the Virgin Islands, with airports, NAVAIDs, communications, weather data sources, special notices, non-regulatory operational procedures and airport diagrams, and data that cannot be readily charted, such as airport hours [[34:199|AIM 9-1-5]]. It was formerly the Airport/Facility Directory [[29:60|IPH 1-44]].

head: IFR question
Where the source says the answer is
rows: Where can I check my VOR?
VOT, ground and airborne checkpoint locations are in the Chart Supplement [[33:71|AIM 1-1-4]].
Is this VOR restricted?
Service volume restrictions appear in NOTAMs, then in the NAVAID listing of the Chart Supplement [[33:73|AIM 1-1-8]].
How do I get a clearance at a non-towered field?
A direct-line phone number to the controlling ATC facility is published there [[29:60|IPH 1-44]].
When is the Class D part-time?
Effective times and the other-times status are in the airport listing [[33:186|AIM 3-2-5]].
Do I need prior permission?
PPRs are typically in the Chart Supplement entry for the airport [[33:397|AIM 5-4-5]].
Is there a TEC route?
Tower En Route Control route descriptions appear in the Chart Supplement [[29:72|IPH 2-12]].
My database is old. Now what?

For IFR, an expired database needs its data verified, and an approach needs proof it was not amended since [[33:101|AIM TBL 1-1-6]]; verify waypoints against current products such as the Chart Supplement [[33:90|AIM 1-1-17]].

body.p: **Availability and revision:** print copies come from FAA-approved print providers, listed with the dates of the latest editions on the AIS website [[34:190|AIM 9-1-2]], and digital Chart Supplements are online [[2:6|Chart Users' Guide p 6]]. To confirm it is current, check the next edition date on the cover [[2:6|Chart Users' Guide p 6]].

callout.text: Application: on the first IFR cross-country lesson, have the learner find the departure airport's VOR checkpoint, the clearance phone number and any PPR, then read you the cover dates.

check.q: Your learner's paper Chart Supplement is 70 days old. Is it current?
check.a: No. The series is issued every 56 days [[34:199|AIM 9-1-5]]; check the next edition date on the cover [[2:6|Chart Users' Guide p 6]].

chunks.title: K6: Standard Instrument Departures and Standard Terminal Arrivals

body.p: Departure procedures (DPs) are preplanned IFR procedures that give obstruction clearance from the terminal area to the en route structure, and there are two types. An ODP, printed textually or graphically, gives obstacle clearance by the least onerous route and may be flown without an ATC clearance unless ATC assigns a SID or radar vectors; a graphic ODP has "(OBSTACLE)" in its title. A SID is an ATC procedure, always graphic, designed mainly to enhance the system and reduce workload, and an ATC clearance must be received before flying it [[33:349|AIM 5-2-9]].

bullets: **Where to find them:** DPs are listed by airport in the IFR Takeoff Minimums and (Obstacle) Departure Procedures section of the TPP, and a "T" on the approach and DP charts sends you there [[33:354|AIM 5-2-9]]. SIDs follow the last approach chart for the airport [[29:42|IPH 1-26]].
**Do not want or cannot fly a SID?** Write "NO SIDs" in the remarks of the flight plan, also when you do not have the chart [[29:42|IPH 1-26]].

**Vectored off:** consider a SID canceled unless ATC adds "expect to resume SID"; when vectored off an ODP or given a lower altitude, the ODP is canceled and ATC takes over terrain and obstacle clearance. The 200 feet per NM climb is always assumed [[33:355|AIM 5-2-9]].

**Part 91 and obstacles:** departing IFR without an ODP, SID or DVA, obstacle clearance is the pilot's job [[33:354|AIM 5-2-9]]; before any IFR departure, consider the terrain, determine whether an ODP exists and whether to fly it [[33:355|AIM 5-2-9]].

body.p: A STAR is an ATC coded IFR arrival route that simplifies clearance delivery and links en route flight to the approach [[33:393|AIM 5-4-1]]. DPs start at the runway and join the en route structure; STARs start in the en route structure and stop short of the runway, mainly because they serve several runways and sometimes several airports [[29:122|IPH 3-10]].

bullets: Using a STAR requires at least the approved chart, and an RNAV STAR must be retrievable by name from the database. Accepting or refusing it is the pilot's call; write "NO STAR" in the remarks [[33:395|AIM 5-4-1]].

"Expect" altitudes and speeds are for planning; they are not crossing restrictions unless ATC issues them, and are not used after a communication failure unless ATC said to expect them [[33:393|AIM 5-4-1]].
Keep the last assigned altitude until cleared to descend; "descend via" authorizes descent to meet the published restrictions [[33:393|AIM 5-4-1]].

body.p: **Availability and revision:** DP and STAR charts are part of the TPP [[34:197|AIM 9-1-5]] and are available from AIS [[33:395|AIM 5-4-1]]; STARs are at the front of each TPP regional booklet [[29:124|IPH 3-12]]. Design criteria change too: Charting Notice 26-03 brought new initial climb area criteria, shown by bolded headers on departure procedures [[2:8|Chart Users' Guide p 8]] [[2:125|Chart Users' Guide p 125]].

callout.text: The most common oral question here: which departure needs a clearance? A SID always; an ODP does not, unless ATC assigns something else [[33:349|AIM 5-2-9]].

check.q: Your learner refuses a STAR because he has only the en route chart. Is that right, and how should he have planned?
check.a: Yes. Using a STAR requires at least the approved chart; he should have written "NO STAR" in the flight plan remarks [[33:395|AIM 5-4-1]].

body.p: IFR en route low altitude charts are for IFR navigation below 18,000 feet MSL. They show airways, limits of controlled airspace, VHF NAVAIDs, airports with terminal communications, MEAs and MOCAs, airway distances, reporting points, special use airspace and military training routes; area charts show congested terminal areas at a larger scale. They are revised every 56 days [[34:194|AIM 9-1-5]]. High altitude charts cover 18,000 feet MSL and above with the jet route structure, also revised every 56 days [[34:195|AIM 9-1-5]].

bullets: The low chart is the instrument equivalent of the sectional. The cover index shows coverage and area charts, and the effective date is printed on the chart [[23:25|IFH 1-6]].
Airport colors: green has an approved approach or radar minima in the TPP or DoD FLIPs; blue, in the high altitude DoD FLIPs; brown, none [[2:63|Chart Users' Guide p 63]].
All airports with an approach are on the low charts; other airports in the contiguous U.S. need a hard-surface runway of at least 3,000 feet [[2:63|Chart Users' Guide p 63]].
Reporting points: an open triangle marks an ATC reporting point; a solid triangle means the report is compulsory [[23:26|IFH 1-7]].
A sideways "T" marks an MEA, MOCA or MAA change away from a NAVAID; the COP symbol shows where to change frequencies [[23:26|IFH 1-7]] [[23:29|IFH 1-10]].

**Availability:** print charts come from FAA-approved print providers, listed with the dates of the latest editions on the AIS website [[34:190|AIM 9-1-2]], and digital IFR charts are online [[2:6|Chart Users' Guide p 6]].

body.p: Tie the chart to the rules: its altitudes are part 95 altitudes [[60:711|14 CFR 95.1(a)]], 91.177 makes them the floor for IFR flight [[60:480|14 CFR 91.177(a)]], and 91.181 makes the airway centerline the course [[60:482|14 CFR 91.181]].

callout.text: Application: teach the legend before the chart. Have the learner unfold the legend panel and decode one airway segment aloud: MEA, MOCA, distance, changeover point, reporting point, then the effective date.

check.q: On an airway with an MEA of 5000 and a MOCA of *3600, your learner wants 4,000 feet to stay out of ice, 35 NM from the VOR, on VOR only. Legal?
check.a: No. Below the MEA down to the MOCA is allowed only with navigation signals, and with VOR only within 22 NM of the VOR [[60:480|14 CFR 91.177(a)]] [[60:712|14 CFR 95.1(e)]]. Ask ATC for a different altitude or route.

chunks.title: K8: Standard instrument approach procedure charts

body.p: An IAP chart shows the data needed to fly an instrument approach: the procedure, navigation data, communications and an airport sketch, each chart built on a specific navigation aid such as ILS, VOR, NDB or RNAV [[34:196|AIM 9-1-5]]. 91.175(a) requires the part 97 SIAP at a civil airport; where military procedures also exist, part 91 pilots must use the civil one, marked "(FAA)" at top center [[33:397|AIM 5-4-5]].

The chart is divided into margin identification, briefing strip, planview, missed approach information, profile view, landing minimums and airport sketch [[2:98|Chart Users' Guide p 98]]. Teach it top to bottom, and teach the currency marks first.

head: Where on the chart
What it tells you
rows: Top margin, above the title
Date of latest revision, a Julian date: year, then day of year; 15344 is day 344 of 2015 [[2:100|Chart Users' Guide p 100]]
Side margins
Volume, current issue date and next issue date, such as SW-3, 21 JUL 2016 to 15 SEP 2016 [[2:100|Chart Users' Guide p 100]]
Bottom left margin
Amendment number and the AIRAC date it took effect; a new amendment means a procedural or criteria change such as a course, fix, altitude or minima [[2:100|Chart Users' Guide p 100]]
Top center
AL number and the responsible organization, such as AL-18 (FAA) [[2:100|Chart Users' Guide p 100]]
Title
From the facility that provides final approach course guidance [[2:100|Chart Users' Guide p 100]]

bullets: The TPP comes in 24 volumes for the conterminous U.S., Puerto Rico and the Virgin Islands; a Change Notice is published at the midpoint between revisions and is free online [[34:196|AIM 9-1-5]], and the digital TPP is online too [[2:6|Chart Users' Guide p 6]].
Approach minimums are based on the local altimeter setting unless the chart says otherwise; if the required setting is not available, the approach is not authorized [[33:399|AIM 5-4-5]].

A pilot who adheres to the charted altitudes, flight paths and minimums, or to radar vectors and altitudes, is assured terrain and obstruction clearance and runway or airport alignment [[33:399|AIM 5-4-5]].
Between editions, check NOTAMs [[2:6|Chart Users' Guide p 6]]; FDC NOTAMs can amend charts and published approaches [[23:293|IFH 10-2]].

callout.text: Application: start every approach briefing with the currency check: side margin dates against today, then the amendment. FII.VIII.A and IR.VI.A cover briefing and flying the approach itself.

check.q: Your learner asks what the side margin "SE-3, 27 NOV 2025 to 25 DEC 2025" on a chart means.
check.a: Volume SE-3, its current issue date and the next issue date [[2:100|Chart Users' Guide p 100]]. On the next issue date a new edition takes over, so check the dates against the day you fly [[2:6|Chart Users' Guide p 6]].

chunks.title: Proving it is current: cycles, 0901Z, notices and databases

body.p: Every document in the flight bag needs a date check, and each one is revised differently. This table pulls the methods of revision together so a learner can prove, document by document, that the bag is current.

head: Document
How it is revised
How to check
rows: En route low and high charts
Effective date printed on the chart [[23:25|IFH 1-6]]
Chart Supplement
Every 56 days [[34:199|AIM 9-1-5]]
Next edition date on the cover [[2:6|Chart Users' Guide p 6]]
TPP: approaches, DPs, STARs
Change Notice at the midpoint between revisions [[34:196|AIM 9-1-5]]
Side margin issue dates, then the amendment [[2:100|Chart Users' Guide p 100]]
Navigation database
28-day revision cycle [[29:263|IPH 6-13]]
Must be current for IFR [[33:92|AIM 1-1-17]]; if expired, verify the data, and fly an approach only if it was not amended since [[33:101|AIM TBL 1-1-6]]
AIM
Basic plus three Changes; next Basic 12/24/26 [[33:52|AIM Table: Publication Schedule]]
Explanation of Changes and Checklist of Pages [[33:37|AIM Explanation of Changes]] [[33:42|AIM Table: Checklist of Pages]]
14 CFR
Amendments in the Federal Register [[60:411|14 CFR 71.1]]
"Up to date as of" date on the eCFR text [[60:711|14 CFR 95.1]]
IFH and IPH
New editions; IFH errata between editions [[23:1|IFH errata note]]
Edition and the edition it superseded, in the preface [[23:6|IFH iii]] [[29:5|IPH iii]]
PTS and ACS
Revised when needed for safety [[FAA-S-8081-9E:7|PTS Concept]]
Edition and date in 61.14 [[60:200|14 CFR 61.14(a)(4)]]

bullets: 0901Z is the changeover time for updated U.S. aeronautical information. Check the effective dates on every chart and publication, use current editions and discard obsolete ones, and check NOTAMs between cycles [[2:6|Chart Users' Guide p 6]].
AIS posts Safety Alerts (errors found in a product), Charting Notices (planned changes) and Data Product Notices (outages and upgrades) on its website [[34:190|AIM 9-1-3]].
A database may not hold every procedure, because the avionics maker decides what to include [[29:263|IPH 6-13]].
An electronic flight bag database must be current to give accurate NAVAID, waypoint and procedure data, just like paper [[23:30|IFH 1-11]].

callout.text: No section in these sources names a chart date, but 91.103 requires the PIC to become familiar with all available information concerning the flight, including for IFR the weather, fuel, alternatives and known delays [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103(a)]]. Teach the date check as part of that duty.

check.q: At what time of day does new aeronautical information take effect in the United States?
check.a: 0901Z, chosen for historically lower traffic so pilots and controllers use the same chart [[2:6|Chart Users' Guide p 6]].

chunks.title: Teaching it: lesson plan, common errors and the checkride

body.p: This Task is all knowledge: you describe each document's purpose, content, availability and revision, related to instrument flight and instruction [[FAA-S-8081-9E:27|PTS II.C]]. Instructional knowledge means explaining it the way the Aviation Instructor's Handbook teaches [[FAA-S-8081-9E:10|PTS Use of the PTS]].

Aim for the correlation level, where the learner links what was taught to other blocks of learning; rote repetition is the lowest level [[25:65|AIH 3-14]] [[25:66|AIH 3-15]]. Here that means going from a chart symbol to its definition, to the rule behind it, and to the date that proves it is current.

bullets: Open with a real scenario: tomorrow's IFR trip. The AIH recommends scenario-based training, with skills integrated into realistic flights [[25:143|AIH 6-12]].
Hand the learner the real documents and let him find each answer. When you do not know, say so and look it up together [[25:143|AIH 6-12]].
Close with a currency drill: every document in the bag, its date, and how to prove it is current. (Application.)

head: Common learner error
Correction
rows: Treats the AIM or the IFH as regulation
Show the AIM policy statement and the IFH preface [[33:53|AIM Flight Information Publication Policy]] [[23:6|IFH iii]]
Thinks an ODP needs a clearance, or a SID does not
Read AIM 5-2-9a together [[33:349|AIM 5-2-9]]
Applies 91.175(f) takeoff minimums to his part 91 flight
Read the paragraph's first sentence [[60:473|14 CFR 91.175(f)]]
Descends to the MOCA far from the VOR
Uses "expect" altitudes after lost communications
Quotes an old handbook name or rule
Check the current source; the A/FD is now the Chart Supplement [[29:60|IPH 1-44]]
Flies with an expired chart or database
Dates on every chart; databases updated for IFR [[2:6|Chart Users' Guide p 6]] [[33:90|AIM 1-1-17]]

callout.text: How the examiner tests it: oral, scenario-based questions that check application and correlation [[FAA-S-8081-9E:13|PTS Evaluator Responsibility]] [[FAA-S-8081-9E:14|PTS Evaluator Responsibility]], such as "Your learner has this chart and this AIM. Is he ready to go?" Bring current documents and show where each answer lives.

check.q: What level of learning should your publications lesson reach, and what does it look like?
check.a: Correlation [[25:66|AIH 3-15]]: the learner goes from a chart symbol to its definition, the rule behind it and the date that proves the chart is current.

scenario.title: The night before the first IFR cross-country
scenario.setup: Your instrument learner, a private pilot with 32 hours of instrument time, plans tomorrow's IFR trip in a club airplane with one VOR and an IFR-approved GPS. The departure airport is non-towered, and its approach charts carry a "T". His tablet chart subscription lapsed three weeks ago. He also has a printed AIM marked Change 2, the club's paper Chart Supplement and a 2012 Instrument Flying Handbook. The airplane's last VOR check was 34 days ago. The destination, which has an ILS, is forecast 1,500 overcast and 4 miles all day.

questions.q: Can he use the charts on his tablet, and how does he prove it?
questions.a: A lapsed subscription means no new data, not automatically expired charts. Check the effective dates on every chart, use current editions and discard obsolete ones [[2:6|Chart Users' Guide p 6]], using the side margin issue dates on each procedure [[2:100|Chart Users' Guide p 100]]. En route charts change every 56 days [[34:194|AIM 9-1-5]], and the GPS database must be current for IFR [[33:90|AIM 1-1-17]].

questions.q: Is his printed AIM good enough to study from?
questions.a: It is out of date: Change 3 has been effective since 7/9/26, and a new Basic follows on 12/24/26 [[33:52|AIM Table: Publication Schedule]]. Change 3 updated IFR paragraphs such as 5-4-5 (approach charts) and 5-5-5 (missed approach) [[33:37|AIM Explanation of Changes]]. The AIM is not regulatory [[33:53|AIM Flight Information Publication Policy]], but he should study the current one.

questions.q: The VOR check is 34 days old. What now?
questions.a: To use the VOR system under IFR he needs a check within the preceding 30 days [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(a)]]. Find a VOT or checkpoint in the Chart Supplement [[33:71|AIM 1-1-4]], make the check within the limits and log date, place, bearing error and signature [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(b)]] [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(d)]].

questions.q: Does he need an alternate, and must he fly the departure procedure?
questions.a: Alternate: yes, the 1,500-foot ceiling is below the 2,000 feet 91.169(b) needs [[60:469|14 CFR 91.169(b)]], so he carries fuel to the destination, the alternate and 45 minutes more [[60:468|14 CFR 91.167(a)(1)]] [[60:469|14 CFR 91.167(a)(2)]]. Departure: 91.175(f) applies to parts 121, 125, 129 and 135 [[60:473|14 CFR 91.175(f)]], but without an ODP or SID obstacle clearance is his responsibility [[33:354|AIM 5-2-9]]. The "T" sends him to the takeoff minimums and departure procedures section of the TPP [[33:354|AIM 5-2-9]], and the AIM strongly encourages flying the DP in IMC [[33:349|AIM 5-2-9]].

questions.q: He asks why he should read a 2012 handbook at all. What do you say?
questions.a: The IFH is the FAA's instrument training reference for instructors and applicants [[23:6|IFH iii]], but some names and rules in it are dated: its A/FD [[23:293|IFH 10-2]] is now the Chart Supplement [[29:60|IPH 1-44]], and currency counts calendar months [[60:239|14 CFR 61.57(c)(1)]]. Use it for technique and check rules against 14 CFR and the AIM; the IPH expands and updates it [[29:5|IPH iii]].

questions.q: In the debrief, what habit do you want him to keep?
questions.a: Before every IFR flight, check the date of every chart, database and publication against the day of the flight, and the NOTAMs in between [[2:6|Chart Users' Guide p 6]]. It is part of becoming familiar with all available information, as 91.103 requires [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103(a)]].

skills.do: Teach "find the IFR rule" aloud: take a learner's question (alternate required? MOCA legal? VOR check good?), go from the Instrument Flight Rules group of part 91 to the section, read its applicability, and answer with the citation and the page open.
skills.practice: Have another applicant fire five questions at you and time each answer; check every answer against the section text [[60:469|14 CFR 91.169(b)]] [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(a)]] [[60:480|14 CFR 91.177(a)]] [[60:473|14 CFR 91.175(f)]].

skills.do: Brief an approach chart as you would to a learner: currency marks first (side margin issue dates, date of latest revision, amendment), then the briefing strip, planview, profile, minimums and airport sketch, tying each part to part 97 and 91.175.
skills.practice: Brief a current chart for your home airport, using the sample chart in this lesson as a model, and explain each margin item from the Chart Users' Guide [[2:98|Chart Users' Guide p 98]] [[2:100|Chart Users' Guide p 100]] [[60:471|14 CFR 91.175(a)]].

quiz.q: Your learner says, "The AIM tells me to do it, so it's a regulation." Which correction is accurate?
options: It is regulatory only for IFR operations inside the NAS
It is not regulatory, but shows procedures other rules may require
It binds pilots once a change has been in effect 30 days
It binds pilots wherever its text uses the word must
quiz.why: The AIM policy statement says it is not regulatory and reflects techniques and procedures that may be requirements in other publications or regulations [[33:53|AIM Flight Information Publication Policy]]. Nothing in it makes it binding for IFR, after a waiting period, or by the word "must".

quiz.q: Today is November 3, 2026. Your learner downloads the AIM to study. Which edition should he be using?
options: Change 3, effective July 9, 2026
Change 2, effective January 22, 2026
The new Basic, effective December 24, 2026
The February 20, 2025 Basic, with no changes
quiz.why: The schedule shows Change 3 effective 7/9/26 and the next Basic not until 12/24/26 [[33:52|AIM Table: Publication Schedule]]. Change 2 has been replaced, and the new Basic is not yet effective.

quiz.q: Your learner, navigating by VOR only, wants to cruise at the MOCA 30 NM from the VOR that defines the airway. What does the rule say?
options: Allowed, since the MOCA gives the same obstacle clearance
Allowed anywhere on the airway as long as he is in VMC
Not allowed: on VOR the MOCA is usable only within 22 NM
Allowed only in areas that are not designated mountainous
quiz.why: 91.177(a)(1) allows flight below the MEA down to the MOCA only with the navigation signals available, and with VOR only within 22 NM of the VOR [[60:480|14 CFR 91.177(a)]]; the MOCA assures VOR reception only within that distance [[60:712|14 CFR 95.1(e)]]. The obstacle clearance is the same, which is why the first option is tempting, but signal coverage is not.

quiz.q: Your learner wants the MEA for a Victor airway on tomorrow's route. Where does he find the number?
options: In the text of 14 CFR part 95, subpart C
In FAA Order JO 7400.11M, incorporated in part 71
In the airport listings of the Chart Supplement
On the IFR en route low altitude chart
quiz.why: The en route low charts show minimum en route and obstruction clearance altitudes [[34:194|AIM 9-1-5]]. Part 95 prescribes the route altitudes, but they are not carried in the CFR text [[60:722|14 CFR 95.31]], and JO 7400.11M lists airspace areas, routes and reporting points [[60:411|14 CFR 71.1]].

quiz.q: Your learner will depart IFR under part 91 from a non-towered field. He asks if he needs a clearance to fly the ODP. Your answer?
options: Yes, every departure procedure needs an ATC clearance
No, unless ATC has assigned a SID or radar vectors instead
Only when the ODP is published as a graphic procedure
Only when the runway has nonstandard takeoff minimums listed
quiz.why: ODPs may be flown without an ATC clearance unless ATC has assigned a SID or radar vectors; it is the SID that needs a clearance [[33:349|AIM 5-2-9]]. Graphic ODPs also need no clearance; they simply carry "(OBSTACLE)" in the title.

quiz.q: A learner asks why ATC keeps giving him STARs into a busy airport. Which answer matches the AIM?
options: Simpler clearances and a link from en route to the approach
Obstacle clearance from the runway up to the en route structure
A replacement for the approach when the weather is VFR
Keeping IFR arrivals below the floor of Class B airspace
quiz.why: A STAR simplifies clearance delivery and eases the transition between en route and approach procedures [[33:393|AIM 5-4-1]]. Obstacle clearance from the terminal area to the en route structure describes departure procedures [[33:349|AIM 5-2-9]].

quiz.q: Which statement about the CFII practical test standard is correct?
options: The CFII test now uses the Instrument Rating ACS, FAA-S-ACS-8C
FAA-S-8081-9D with Changes 1 and 2 is still the current edition
FAA-S-8081-9E, November 2023, is incorporated into part 61
The PTS is guidance, so the evaluator may skip its tasks
quiz.why: 61.14(a)(4) incorporates FAA-S-8081-9E, November 2023 [[60:200|14 CFR 61.14(a)(4)]], and the practical test consists of its tasks [[60:222|14 CFR 61.43(a)(1)]]. FAA-S-ACS-8C is the instrument rating ACS [[60:200|14 CFR 61.14(b)(5)]], and 9E superseded 9D [[FAA-S-8081-9E:2|PTS Foreword]].

quiz.q: Your learner points to the number in the top margin of this chart. What does 15344 tell him?
options: The procedure has been amended 344 times since 2015
The AL number that identifies this procedure
The volume expires 344 days after it is issued
The chart was last revised on day 344 of 2015
quiz.why: The date of latest revision in the top margin is a Julian date: the first two digits are the year, the last three the day of the year [[2:100|Chart Users' Guide p 100]]. The AL number is a separate item at top center, and amendments are shown in the bottom margin.

quiz.q: Your learner's check at a VOR ground checkpoint shows a 5-degree error. What do you teach?
options: Fly IFR; a ground checkpoint allows 6 degrees
No IFR on the VOR until the error is corrected
Fly IFR and add 5 degrees to every bearing
Fly IFR after logging the error in the record
quiz.why: A ground checkpoint allows plus or minus 4 degrees [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(b)]]; 6 degrees is the airborne limit. With a larger error IFR flight must not be attempted until the source is corrected, and no correction other than the manufacturer's correction card may be applied [[33:71|AIM 1-1-4]].

quiz.q: The destination has an ILS and is forecast 2,500 broken and 5 miles from 1 hour before to 1 hour after ETA. Is an alternate required?
options: Required, because every IFR flight plan lists one
Required, because the ceiling is below 3,000 feet
Not required: an approach, 2,000 feet and 3 miles
Not required, but only if the destination has a tower
quiz.why: 91.169(b) removes the alternate requirement when part 97 prescribes an approach at the destination and, from 1 hour before to 1 hour after ETA, the ceiling will be at least 2,000 feet and visibility at least 3 statute miles [[60:469|14 CFR 91.169(b)]]. Nothing in the rule depends on a tower.

quiz.q: Where does your learner find the locations of VOTs and VOR checkpoints?
options: In 14 CFR 91.171, with the tolerances
In the legend of the en route low chart
In the AIM chapter 1 tables
In the Chart Supplement
quiz.why: Locations of airborne and ground checkpoints and VOTs are published in the Chart Supplement [[33:71|AIM 1-1-4]]. 91.171 sets the check and its limits but lists no locations [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(b)]].

quiz.q: Departure control vectors your learner off the SID he was cleared for. What should he assume?
options: The SID is canceled unless ATC says to expect to resume it
The SID altitude restrictions apply until he reaches the MEA
He must rejoin the SID at the next fix on his own
The SID speed limits still apply until he leaves 10,000
quiz.why: Vectored or cleared off a SID, pilots must consider it canceled unless the controller adds "expect to resume SID", and its published altitude and speed restrictions are canceled too [[33:355|AIM 5-2-9]].

final_quiz.q: Which part of 14 CFR designates the Class E airspace that begins at 700 feet AGL around an airport with an instrument approach?
options: Part 71, airspace designations
Part 91, general operating rules
Part 95, IFR altitudes and mountainous areas
Part 97, standard instrument procedures
final_quiz.why: 71.71(c) designates Class E from 700 feet or more above the surface with an airport that has an approved instrument approach [[60:416|14 CFR 71.71(c)]]. Part 91 sets operating rules in that airspace, while parts 95 and 97 hold altitudes and procedures.

final_quiz.q: Your learner prints part 97 to study the ILS at his home airport. What will he find?
options: The full ILS procedure with its minimums, by airport
Only the military procedures, since civil ones are in the AIM
Terms and general rules; the procedures are on FAA forms
Nothing; approaches are listed in part 95 with the MEAs
final_quiz.why: Part 97 holds only general sections: applicability, terms and bearings [[60:723|14 CFR 97.1]] [[60:725|14 CFR 97.5(a)]], and the TERPS basis; the procedures themselves are documented on FAA Forms 8260-3, -4 and -5, incorporated by reference, and depicted on FAA charts [[60:726|14 CFR 97.20]]. Editorial notes confirm the procedures are not carried in the CFR [[60:726|14 CFR 97.20]].

final_quiz.q: An airplane's VREF is 118 knots. Which approach category does 97.3 give it?
options: A, below 91 knots
B, 91 to under 121 knots
C, 121 to under 141 knots
D, 141 to under 166 knots
final_quiz.why: Category B is 91 knots or more but less than 121 knots, based on VREF, or 1.3 VSO if no VREF is specified [[60:724|14 CFR 97.3]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner reads that the IFH says a pilot "must" do something. How binding is that?
options: Fully binding, because the IFH is an FAA handbook
Binding only during the instrument practical test
Binding once it is repeated in the AIM
Not binding: the IFH says it adds no duty to 14 CFR rules
final_quiz.why: The IFH preface says its "must" language is not intended to add to, interpret or relieve a duty imposed by 14 CFR [[23:6|IFH iii]]. Repeating it in the AIM would not make it binding either, since the AIM is not regulatory [[33:53|AIM Flight Information Publication Policy]].

final_quiz.q: How is the Instrument Flying Handbook kept current between editions?
options: An errata sheet online, fixed in the next version
Change pages issued on the AIM schedule
Reissued every 56 days with the charts
Corrections published as FDC NOTAMs
final_quiz.why: An errata sheet on the FAA handbooks page lists content and grammar errors, to be corrected in the next version [[23:1|IFH errata note]]; a new edition supersedes the old one [[23:6|IFH iii]]. Change pages on a schedule are how the AIM is revised [[33:52|AIM Table: Publication Schedule]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner's paper Chart Supplement is 70 days old. What do you tell him?
options: Still good until the next AIM change is published
Good for one year from its printed date
Replaced: the series is issued every 56 days
Good until an FDC NOTAM cancels it
final_quiz.why: The Chart Supplement is issued every 56 days [[34:199|AIM 9-1-5]], and the next edition date is on the cover [[2:6|Chart Users' Guide p 6]]. It is not tied to the AIM schedule.

final_quiz.q: Which statement about departure procedures is correct?
options: An ODP needs a clearance; a SID can be flown without one
A SID is always graphic, and it needs an ATC clearance first
Both types need an ATC clearance before takeoff
An ODP is designed mainly to reduce controller workload
final_quiz.why: SIDs are always printed graphically and an ATC clearance must be received before flying one; ODPs may be textual or graphic and may be flown without a clearance unless ATC assigns something else [[33:349|AIM 5-2-9]]. Reducing workload is the main purpose of a SID, not an ODP [[2:124|Chart Users' Guide p 124]].

final_quiz.q: On a STAR, ATC says "descend via the arrival." Your learner asks what that allows.
options: An immediate descent to the lowest altitude on the STAR
Descent to the printed expect altitudes only
Lateral navigation only, at the last assigned altitude
Pilot's discretion descent to meet the restrictions
final_quiz.why: "Descend via" authorizes descent at pilot's discretion to meet published restrictions while navigating the STAR [[33:393|AIM 5-4-1]]. "Expect" altitudes are planning information, not restrictions, unless ATC issues them [[33:393|AIM 5-4-1]].

final_quiz.q: On the en route low chart an airport symbol is brown. What does that tell your learner?
options: No published approach or radar minima there
An approach published only in the DoD FLIPs
A control tower that operates only part of the day
A Class D surface area around the airport
final_quiz.why: Brown marks airports without a published instrument approach procedure or radar minima; green and blue mark airports with them [[2:63|Chart Users' Guide p 63]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner's IFR GPS database expired yesterday. What does the AIM require before he uses it under IFR?
options: Nothing until the next 56-day chart cycle begins
Nothing for 28 days, the length of one data cycle
Verify its data, and fly approaches only if unamended
A new database for en route; approaches may still be flown
final_quiz.why: With an expired database, IFR en route and terminal use requires verifying the data for correctness, and an approach requires a current database or verification that the procedure has not been amended since the database expired; check the AFM supplement for the unit's approvals and limitations [[33:101|AIM TBL 1-1-6]]. The simple rule to teach is that databases must be updated for IFR [[33:90|AIM 1-1-17]]. The 28 days is the database revision cycle [[29:263|IPH 6-13]], not a grace period.

final_quiz.q: Which section requires an instrument rating on your flight instructor certificate to give the training for an instrument rating?
final_quiz.why: 61.195(c) sets the instrument rating requirement for instructors giving instrument training [[60:346|14 CFR 61.195(c)]]. 61.57(c) is pilot currency, 61.65(b) the learner's knowledge areas, and 91.109(c) the safety pilot.

final_quiz.q: During an IPC, which regulations and charts does AC 61-98E have you check?
options: Only the 61.57 currency rules and the pilot's own logbook
Part 91 B, C and E; en route, SID, ODP, STAR and IAP charts
Part 61 Subpart H and the flight instructor's training records
Part 71 and the airspace listings in JO 7400.11M
final_quiz.why: The IPC knowledge portion covers part 91, especially Subparts B, C and E, and the interpretation of en route and approach charts including SIDs, ODPs, STARs and IAPs [[15:31|AC 61-98E 5.2.1]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner wants to know what changed in the newest AIM. Where should he look first?
options: The Pilot/Controller Glossary
The What's New page of the Chart Users' Guide
The Explanation of Changes at its front
The reference list in FAA-S-8081-9E
final_quiz.why: Each AIM Basic and Change opens with an Explanation of Changes listing the changed paragraphs and why [[33:37|AIM Explanation of Changes]]. The Chart Users' Guide What's New page covers chart changes, not the AIM [[2:8|Chart Users' Guide p 8]].

final_quiz.q: How do the part 71 airspace listings change?
options: Federal Register rules, then a new JO 7400.11 edition
Through the AIM Changes on the published AIM schedule
Through Charting Notices posted on the AIS website
Through special notices printed in the Chart Supplement
final_quiz.why: Proposed and final changes to the listings are published in the Federal Register and periodically integrated into a revised edition of the Order, which is then incorporated by reference [[60:411|14 CFR 71.1]]. Charting Notices announce chart enhancements, not airspace rules [[34:190|AIM 9-1-3]].

final_quiz.q: Looking at this chart, how does your learner confirm it is current for a flight tomorrow?
options: Check that the amendment is less than a year old
Compare both side margin issue dates with tomorrow's date
Compare the MSA with the MEA on the en route chart
Find the airport elevation in the Chart Supplement
final_quiz.why: The side margins show the current issue date and the next issue date [[2:100|Chart Users' Guide p 100]], and pilots should check effective dates and use current editions [[2:6|Chart Users' Guide p 6]]. An amendment date shows when the procedure last changed, not whether this chart edition is current.

takeaways: Rule first, help second: 14 CFR and what it incorporates bind; the AIM, IFH and IPH help you comply.
Parts 95 and 97 point to altitudes and procedures you read on charts; 91.177 and 91.175 make them binding.
Part 71's airspace lives in FAA Order JO 7400.11M, re-incorporated about once a year.
AIM: a Basic and three Changes. Today it is Change 3; the next Basic starts 12/24/26. Read the Explanation of Changes.
En route charts and the Chart Supplement: 56 days; approach charts: read the side margin dates; 0901Z, NOTAMs in between; databases every 28 days.
ODP: no clearance needed. SID: clearance required. STAR: approved chart required.
On every approach chart, check the side margin dates, the revision date and the amendment.
Teach to correlation: chart symbol, definition, rule, and the date that proves it is current.
cfi_notes: How it is tested: the FAA-S-8081-9E Area II note has the evaluator select Tasks A and D and at least one other [[FAA-S-8081-9E:26|PTS Area II NOTE]], and its table for adding an instrument rating to a flight instructor certificate lists Area II Tasks A and C for holders of an airplane rating, and a Task listed there is mandatory [[FAA-S-8081-9E:18|PTS Additional Rating Table]]. A CFI-airplane adding the instrument rating will be tested on this Task.

The IFH (2012) uses names that have changed: the Airport/Facility Directory and AeroNav Products [[23:293|IFH 10-2]] [[23:25|IFH 1-6]]. The Chart Supplement replaced the A/FD [[29:60|IPH 1-44]], and AIS now produces the charts [[34:190|AIM 9-1-1]]. Teach the current names, and check any other planning source the IFH names (its list includes the NTAP and DUATS) against the current AIM before teaching it.

Two dated IFH details: its introduction says currency tasks are done "within the preceding 6 months" and the IPC uses the instrument PTS [[23:11|IFH viii]], while 61.57 uses 6 calendar months and the ACS [[60:239|14 CFR 61.57(c)(1)]] [[60:240|14 CFR 61.57(d)(1)]]; and it puts the julian date after the amendment number in the bottom margin [[23:31|IFH 1-12]], while the current Chart Users' Guide puts the date of latest revision in the top margin and the amendment with its AIRAC date at the bottom [[2:100|Chart Users' Guide p 100]]. Teach the regulation and the Chart Users' Guide.

The AIM speaks two ways about GPS databases: 1-1-17 says they must be updated (current) for IFR [[33:90|AIM 1-1-17]] [[33:92|AIM 1-1-17]], but the notes to TBL 1-1-6 allow IFR en route and terminal use of an expired database after verifying the data, and an approach after verifying the procedure has not been amended [[33:101|AIM TBL 1-1-6]]. Teach updating as the habit and the verification rule as the exception, within the AFM supplement's limits.

The 2010 TPP page in IFH Figure 1-8 carries a civil users note about part 91 takeoff minimums for certain operators [[23:32|IFH 1-13]]; current 91.175(f) applies its takeoff minimums to parts 121, 125, 129 and 135 [[60:473|14 CFR 91.175(f)]]. Learners who read old figures get this wrong.

AIM 5-2-9g calls the takeoff minimums and departure procedures section "Section L" of the TPP and, a few lines later, says the "T" symbol refers users to "Section C" [[33:354|AIM 5-2-9]] [[33:355|AIM 5-2-9]]. Teach the section by its title, IFR Takeoff Minimums and (Obstacle) Departure Procedures.
The AIM Publication Schedule prints the next Change 1 effective date as "6/10727" [[33:52|AIM Table: Publication Schedule]]. Confirm the date on the FAA publications page when it matters.

FAA-S-8081-9E still says all instrument rating PTS procedures are included in it [[FAA-S-8081-9E:9|PTS Use of the PTS]], but the instrument rating and IPC now use FAA-S-ACS-8C [[60:200|14 CFR 61.14(b)(5)]]. Even AC 61-98E (2024) still names the "A/FD" in its IPC knowledge list [[15:32|AC 61-98E 5.2.1]].

The IFH says blue or green airport symbols on en route charts have approaches [[23:25|IFH 1-6]]; the Chart Users' Guide defines green as an approach or radar minima in the TPP or DoD FLIPs and blue as published in the high altitude DoD FLIPs [[2:63|Chart Users' Guide p 63]]. For civil airports, teach green.
gaps: No source here states the revision cycle of the conterminous U.S. TPP. The AIM gives 56 days only for the Alaska TPP and says a Change Notice comes at the midpoint between revisions [[34:196|AIM 9-1-5]] [[34:197|AIM 9-1-5]]; the Chart Users' Guide sample margins show a 56-day span in its text and a 28-day span on its sample chart [[2:100|Chart Users' Guide p 100]] [[2:98|Chart Users' Guide p 98]]. Read the side margin dates.
No source here says how often the FAA revises its handbooks; only new editions and the IFH errata sheet are described.

No source here says whether a part 91 pilot must carry charts, paper or electronic, or names a chart currency rule by date; the IFH remark on electronic flight bags concerns operators with FAA approval [[23:30|IFH 1-11]].
The Federal Register process and the List of CFR Sections Affected are named in 14 CFR [[60:722|14 CFR 95.31]] but not explained in these sources.

cards.s: The IFH's "must" wording adds requirements to 14 CFR.
cards.why: False. The preface says it does not add to, interpret or relieve a 14 CFR duty [[23:6|IFH iii]].

cards.s: The AIM is posted on the FAA website by its effective date and sent to email subscribers.
The AIM is revised every 56 days, together with the charts.
cards.why: False. It is a Basic manual plus three Changes on a published schedule [[33:52|AIM Table: Publication Schedule]].

cards.s: Each AIM change opens with an Explanation of Changes.
The IPH expands and updates information in the IFH.
Part 97 prints every standard instrument approach procedure in the CFR.
cards.why: False. The procedures are on incorporated FAA forms and FAA charts [[60:726|14 CFR 97.20]].

cards.s: Bearings and radials in part 71 are magnetic.
cards.why: False. They are true [[60:412|14 CFR 71.7]]; part 97 courses are magnetic [[60:725|14 CFR 97.5(a)]].

items.q: At a VOT, with the CDI centered and a TO indication, the OBS reads 183 degrees. What is the bearing error in degrees?
items.why: With the CDI centered on a VOT the OBS should read 180 with TO [[33:70|AIM 1-1-4]]: 183 - 180 = 3, inside the plus or minus 4 degree limit [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(b)]].

items.q: Dual VORs tuned to the same station read 052 and 057 degrees. What is the variation in degrees?
items.why: 057 - 052 = 5, more than the 4 degrees allowed between dual systems [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(c)]].

items.q: No minimum altitude is published for an off-route leg in a non-mountainous area. The highest obstacle within 4 NM of the course is 2,350 feet MSL. What is the lowest IFR altitude, in feet MSL?
items.why: 1,000 feet above the highest obstacle within 4 NM: 2,350 + 1,000 = 3,350 [[60:480|14 CFR 91.177(a)]].

items.q: Same leg, but in a designated mountainous area with the highest obstacle at 6,820 feet MSL. Lowest IFR altitude, in feet MSL?
items.why: 2,000 feet above the highest obstacle within 4 NM in a part 95 mountainous area: 6,820 + 2,000 = 8,820 [[60:480|14 CFR 91.177(a)]].

items.q: The airplane burns 9.6 gallons per hour at normal cruise. How many gallons is the 91.167 reserve after reaching the alternate?
items.why: 45 minutes at normal cruising speed is 0.75 hour: 0.75 x 9.6 = 7.2 gallons [[60:469|14 CFR 91.167(a)(3)]].

activities.title: The evening before the IFR trip
activities.intro: Your instrument learner plans tomorrow's first IFR cross-country with you. Make each call as the evening unfolds.

steps.s: 1900. His tablet chart subscription lapsed three weeks ago, but the app still opens the approach charts.
options: Use them; a chart stays good until the next AIM change
Use them, since any part 97 chart meets 91.175(a) forever
Print the old charts so they no longer depend on the app
Check the issue dates and database date, then update
steps.why: Check effective dates on every chart and use current editions [[2:6|Chart Users' Guide p 6]], using the side margin issue dates [[2:100|Chart Users' Guide p 100]]; the database must be current for IFR [[33:90|AIM 1-1-17]].

steps.s: 1915. The departure airport's approach charts carry a "T". He plans to depart IFR into a 600-foot overcast.
options: Read the TPP takeoff section and plan to fly any ODP
Ignore it; the T applies only to airline flights
Call ATC tomorrow for a clearance to fly the ODP
Turn on course right after takeoff using standard minimums
steps.why: The "T" points to the IFR takeoff minimums and (obstacle) departure procedures section [[33:354|AIM 5-2-9]]. Without an ODP or SID, obstacle clearance is his responsibility [[33:354|AIM 5-2-9]], and the AIM strongly encourages a DP in IMC [[33:349|AIM 5-2-9]]. An ODP needs no clearance [[33:349|AIM 5-2-9]].

steps.s: 1930. The airplane's VOR check is 34 days old, and he plans to fly the Victor airways on the VOR.
options: Fly it, because the GPS can stand in for the VOR check
Do a VOT or checkpoint check before departure and log it
Ask maintenance to extend the old check by 30 days
Fly it, because the check only matters for VOR approaches
steps.why: Using the VOR system under IFR needs a check within the preceding 30 days, logged with date, place, bearing error and signature [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(a)]] [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(d)]]. Locations are in the Chart Supplement [[33:71|AIM 1-1-4]].

steps.s: 1945. Destination forecast: 1,500 overcast and 4 miles from 2 hours before to 2 hours after ETA. It has an ILS.
options: No alternate, because the destination has an ILS
No alternate, because the visibility is over 3 miles
File an alternate and carry fuel to it plus 45 minutes
File an alternate, but plan no extra fuel to reach it
steps.why: The ceiling is below the 2,000 feet 91.169(b) needs, so an alternate is required [[60:469|14 CFR 91.169(b)]], and fuel must cover the destination, the alternate and 45 minutes [[60:468|14 CFR 91.167(a)(1)]] [[60:469|14 CFR 91.167(a)(2)]].

steps.s: 2000. He asks which AIM to read tonight: his printed Change 2 or the FAA website.
options: Change 2 is fine until the next Basic on 12/24/26
The website, where the current edition is Change 3
Either one, since the AIM is not regulatory anyway
Neither; wait for the 12/24/26 Basic to be published
steps.why: Change 3 has been effective since 7/9/26 [[33:52|AIM Table: Publication Schedule]], and the AIM is posted on the FAA website by its effective date [[33:50|AIM Subscription Information]]. Not being regulatory [[33:53|AIM Flight Information Publication Policy]] does not make an old edition good enough.
